title: Lindblad theory of linear response susceptibility and dispersive readout in minimal Kitaev junctions
authors: Tobias Kuhn, Raffael L. Klees, Ramón Aguado, Mónica Benito
abstract: The field of hybrid superconductor-semiconductor quantum dots is advancing toward the development of functional devices that leverage the advantages of both types of materials. However, the inherent complexity of these devices demands a comprehensive theoretical framework for a complete understanding of their responses to external probes, readout and the dissipation arising from environmental coupling. We present a Lindblad-based linear response formalism that captures the multi-level nature of these devices, their probe-readout flexibility, and the non-unitary effects of finite-frequency response, including the so-called Sisyphus and Hermes dynamical susceptibilities. These arise from fluctuations in the rates and jump operators, and are hence absent in standard Kubo linear response treatments. We exemplify the framework using quantum dot-based Kitaev chain setups which are promising candidates for topologically protected Majorana-based parity qubits. Our results shed light onto the validity of the standard curvature-based approximation for fermionic parity and qubit readout, show that Hermes terms compensate decoherence in dispersive readout and implement important corrections beyond thermalized states.
summary: This paper introduces a sophisticated Lindblad-based linear response formalism to accurately characterize the electrical response of complex hybrid superconductor-semiconductor quantum dots. It moves beyond standard Kubo treatments by incorporating non-unitary effects via 'Hermes' and 'Sisyphus' susceptibilities. The theory is demonstrated on Kitaev chain models, showing how these advanced terms are crucial for correctly interpreting measurements like qubit readout fidelity.
main_problem: The paper addresses the need for a comprehensive theoretical framework to understand the response of complex hybrid superconductor-semiconductor quantum dots (SCQDs) to external probes and environmental dissipation.
main_result: It demonstrates that a full Lindblad linear response formalism is necessary, showing that contributions like 'Hermes' terms compensate decoherence effects in dispersive readout and provide corrections beyond simple thermalized state approximations.
method: The authors develop and apply a Lindblad-based linear response formalism to calculate the system susceptibility ($\chi$), decomposing it into static, Hamiltonian, Sisyphus, and Hermes contributions.
model_or_system: The primary model is hybrid SCQD devices, exemplified by quantum dot-based Kitaev chain setups used for Majorana-based parity qubits. Dynamics are governed by a Lindblad master equation, and the analysis focuses on calculating susceptibility components derived from this formalism.
key_observables: Linear-response susceptibility ($\chi(\omega)$), Quantum Capacitance ($C_Q$), static susceptibility ($\chi_{st}$), Hamiltonian contribution ($\chi_H$), Sisyphus susceptibility ($\chi_\Gamma$), and Hermes susceptibility ($\chi_L$).
important_parameters: Frequency ($\omega$), temperature ($T$), coupling strength ($\Delta, t$), and detuning parameters.
main_assumptions: The derivation relies on the Born-Markov approximations (weakly coupled environment with no memory) and analyzes the system within the linear response regime.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate parameter fluctuations contributing to observables, compare various susceptibility terms ($\chi_{st}, \chi_H, \chi_\Gamma, \chi_L$) against theoretical predictions like band curvature, and show parity state differentiation in common gate spectroscopy.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the general Lindblad linear response formalism for N-level systems. It then applies this theory to minimal Kitaev junctions, deriving specific expressions for the four susceptibility components ($\chi_{st}, \chi_H, \chi_\Gamma, \chi_L$). Finally, it analyzes these contributions in the context of quantum capacitance and parity state spectroscopy.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant to AMO physics and open quantum systems as it provides advanced tools (Lindblad response theory) to model dissipation and measurement back-action in solid-state quantum devices like superconducting qubits.
